newsitem.title: INDIA: India concern on Pakistan persists after Jiang trip.
newsitem.headline: India concern on Pakistan persists after Jiang trip.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin's visit to India yielded positive results but concerns remained over China's ties with Pakistan, India's traditional rival.

Jiang's visit, the first to India by a Chinese president, was a major step towards healing old scars in ties between the the world's two most populous nations, which fought a brief Himalayan border war in 1962, analysts said.
"The visit was a positive event as far as bilateral relations are concerned," K. Natwar Singh, a former minister and diplomat, told Reuters.
"Jiang is the only Chinese leader after Mao to hold all the three offices of head of state, party general secretary and chairman of the military commission," he added.
Rasheed Talib, an independent political commentator, said he did not read too much into Jiang's visit, although it yielded some positive results.
Jiang left New Delhi for Pakistan on Sunday. In India, both sides signed an agreement that aimed to reduce tension along their border, and could lead to troop and weapon cutbacks.
On Jiang's Pakistan trip, Talib said: "The Chinese always do this balancing act.
"Partly the move towards India is meant to the impress the U.S. -- as a move towards an Asian identity -- and then he goes off to Pakistan to maintain the balance," he added.
India and Pakistan, born out of a bloody partition during independence from Britain in 1947, have fought three wars.
Recent media reports said China sold nuclear weapon-related equipment to Pakistan, in breach of U.S. and global arms control pacts. Both sides have denied this.

"The Chinese government does not, did not, and will not sell or transfer any nuclear weapon or technology to any country," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told reporters in New Delhi after Jiang's official talks on Friday.
But the denials have not soothed Indian concerns.

"Although sceptics might say the talks did not result in reassurance to India that Chinese nuclear assistance or missile technology would not be available to Pakistan, there was a great deal to derive comfort from in the agreement," the Times of Indian quoted an unnamed foreign ministry official as saying.
Natwar Singh said India made clear to Jiang that it viewed the prospect of China giving military aid and nuclear technology to Pakistan with great concern.
"But this is only a minor hurdle in completely normalising relations," he added.
Other agreements signed during the visit included allowing an Indian consulate office in Hong Kong after the colony reverts to China in mid-1997, and a shipping pact.
Talib said China had always been closer to Pakistan than to India, especially since the 1962 war. "India wants to cock a snook at both the U.S. and Pakistan by cozying up to China," he said.
"But that's a bit of wishful thinking, since (Jiang) Zemin is going to Pakistan and is going to say exactly the opposite thing there."
